name: Broken Object-Level Authorization
scenario: Alice and Bob maintain separate support requests. Bob's renewal ticket must remain private to Bob and support staff.
objective: Distinguish a valid session from permission to a particular object.
steps: Sign in as alice in each application.
Open /tickets/2 and request GET /api/tickets/2.
Attempt PATCH /api/tickets/2 with status closed using Alice's own CSRF token.
Confirm Alice can still read and update ticket 1.
expected: Training returns Bob's synthetic renewal and accepts its update; hardened returns 404 for both API and HTML access and rejects mutation.
root_cause: TrainingPolicy.ticket returns True without comparing owner_id to the authenticated user.
remediation: SecurePolicy.ticket checks ownership or an explicit support role; every ticket read, update, comment and attachment-list route invokes the shared authorization function.
residual: Support employees intentionally access all tickets. This is a documented business permission, not tenant isolation for support staff.

name: Unauthorized File Access
scenario: A private renewal document belongs to Bob's ticket, but a download endpoint accepts its numeric identifier.
objective: Authorize file downloads through the owning business object.
steps: Sign in as alice.
Request GET /api/attachments/2 in each application.
Download /api/attachments/1 to verify legitimate access.
Inspect Content-Disposition and Content-Type on successful downloads.
expected: Training reveals Bob's synthetic document; hardened returns 404. Alice's own text document downloads in both.
root_cause: TrainingPolicy.attachment checks neither ticket ownership nor the requester's role.
remediation: Resolve the attachment's parent ticket and apply the same object policy before reading content. Return downloads as text/plain attachments with nosniff.
residual: Attachment identifiers are enumerable by design. Authorization, rather than identifier secrecy, provides the boundary.

name: Vertical Privilege Escalation
scenario: Only administrators can assign support requests. The customer interface hides the assignment form.
objective: Prove that hidden UI controls do not enforce a role boundary.
steps: Sign in as alice and observe that /tickets/1 has no assignment form.
POST /api/admin/tickets/1/assign with assignee_id 3 and Alice's CSRF token.
Repeat as admin to verify the legitimate administrative workflow.
expected: Training accepts Alice's direct request despite the hidden form; hardened returns 403. A real admin can assign in both.
root_cause: TrainingPolicy.admin always permits the call. Presentation-layer role checks cannot protect a direct HTTP endpoint.
remediation: The shared administrator dependency applies a server-side admin role check and records denials before any state change.
residual: The training bypass affects ticket assignment only. Role mutation and audit export retain real admin checks as safety boundaries.

name: SQL Injection
scenario: The support queue searches ticket titles while limiting customer results to their own tickets.
objective: Explain how SQL parameter binding separates syntax from data.
steps: Sign in as alice and search normally for Workspace.
GET /api/tickets with q set to ' OR 1=1 -- (URL encode the parameter).
Compare returned owner IDs in the two variants.
Use only this read-only boolean payload against synthetic fixtures.
expected: Training returns Bob's ticket because input changes the WHERE clause. Hardened treats the whole payload as literal search text and returns no matching tickets.
root_cause: TrainingPolicy.search interpolates the search term into SQL source. The injected OR predicate bypasses the ownership condition.
remediation: SecurePolicy.search builds SQLAlchemy expressions and binds values. It also escapes LIKE wildcards so literal searches remain predictable.
residual: The demonstration runs in a separate read-only PostgreSQL transaction using a restricted runtime role. SQLite tests do not establish that PostgreSQL boundary.

name: Stored Cross-Site Scripting
scenario: A support comment persists in the database and is later rendered in a conversation.
objective: Observe stored script execution and verify escaped output in a real browser.
steps: Sign in as alice and add the harmless comment <script>document.body.dataset.proof='stored'</script> to ticket 1.
Reload /tickets/1 in Chromium.
Inspect document.body.dataset.proof and the visible comment text.
Run the explicit browser suite for execution evidence.
expected: Training sets the local DOM marker stored. Hardened displays the input as text, creates no script element from the comment, and never sets the marker.
root_cause: TrainingPolicy.render marks untrusted comments as trusted HTML, bypassing Jinja's escaping.
remediation: Escape HTML at the final render boundary. Keep scripts in same-origin static files and apply a restrictive CSP as defense in depth.
residual: The proof changes only a browser-local DOM attribute. API text comparisons alone do not prove browser execution or prevention.

name: Reflected Cross-Site Scripting
scenario: A search feedback page echoes the supplied query into its HTML response.
objective: Recognize a reflected HTML injection sink and apply context-aware encoding.
steps: Sign in and open /search with q set to <script>document.body.dataset.proof='reflected'</script>.
Inspect the browser-local DOM marker.
Verify the hardened response displays literal angle brackets without inserting an executable element.
expected: The training page executes the harmless marker script. The hardened page renders it as text.
root_cause: The training policy returns Markup for the unescaped query, turning input data into document structure.
remediation: Encode the query for an HTML text-node context at the final output step; avoid assigning untrusted values to innerHTML.
residual: The supported echo context is an HTML text node. This lesson does not establish encoding correctness for every possible JavaScript or CSS sink.

name: Cross-Site Request Forgery
scenario: An authenticated customer updates a display name through a state-changing form request.
objective: Distinguish browser site boundaries, origin boundaries, and CSRF tokens.
steps: Authenticate in each variant.
From a different loopback port, submit a form POST to /api/profile with display_name=Forged Local Name and no token.
Observe the response and profile state.
Repeat a legitimate update with the session's X-CSRF-Token header.
expected: The training profile changes. Hardened returns 403 and retains its original display name; the valid token update succeeds.
root_cause: TrainingPolicy.csrf does nothing, allowing an ambient session cookie to authorize an unsolicited form.
remediation: Validate a per-session synchronizer token using a constant-time comparison, validate Origin when supplied, and use HttpOnly SameSite=Lax cookies.
residual: Different loopback ports are cross-origin but same-site; this intentionally demonstrates why SameSite alone is insufficient. Local HTTP cookies lack Secure until TLS is configured.

name: Authentication Weaknesses
scenario: An attacker with no account compares failed login responses and repeats a small bounded fixture sequence.
objective: Verify consistent failure messages and controlled attempt throttling.
steps: POST a wrong password for alice and for nonexistent-user.
Compare status and response text.
Make at most six wrong attempts for one synthetic username.
Reset or wait 60 seconds, then verify a normal login.
expected: Training distinguishes unknown user from wrong password and accepts all bounded attempts. Hardened returns identical 401 errors before its threshold, then 429.
root_cause: TrainingPolicy.login_error reveals account existence and its rate_limit omits attempt accounting.
remediation: Use an equal-format response and dummy Argon2 verification for unknown users, persist account/client attempt buckets, and issue fresh opaque server-side sessions.
residual: Single-process throttling is suitable for the one-worker lab, not a distributed rate limiter. Timing tests do not prove constant-time end-to-end behavior. Fixture credentials are intentionally public.

name: Insecure Session Management
scenario: An employee signs out, but an earlier copy of their session cookie may still be replayed.
objective: Verify backend invalidation rather than trusting cookie deletion.
steps: Sign in as sam and retain the synthetic session cookie in memory only.
POST /api/logout with the correct CSRF token.
Replay the old cookie to GET /api/session.
Check fresh login rotation, expiry, invalid cookies and role-change invalidation in regression tests.
expected: Training accepts the logged-out cookie. Hardened returns 401 and also rejects expired or invalidated sessions.
root_cause: TrainingPolicy.revoke deletes no server record; the browser's cookie removal does not invalidate a stolen reference token.
remediation: Store only token hashes, delete backend sessions on logout, rotate on login, expire sessions, and compare a user's current session version after privilege changes.
residual: Reference tokens remain bearer credentials until invalidated. Cookies for the two variants have distinct names because cookies do not isolate by port.

name: Unsafe File Upload Handling
scenario: A customer attaches a text document, supplying an unexpected extension, path-like filename, or excessive content.
objective: Validate filenames and content while keeping storage independent of user paths.
steps: Upload harmless text with filename ../notes.csv to ticket 1.
Try a 65537-byte text document and UTF-8-invalid bytes.
Upload a normal small notes.txt and download it.
Never upload executable code; all stored content remains inert database bytes.
expected: Training accepts unsafe metadata and files above the hardened size limit up to its safety ceiling. Hardened rejects them and accepts valid small UTF-8 .txt documents with generated storage keys.
root_cause: TrainingPolicy.upload retains the raw filename and skips extension, content and strict size validation.
remediation: Canonicalize and validate names, accept only bounded UTF-8 text, use random storage identifiers, and force text/plain attachment downloads.
residual: Files are database blobs, not filesystem writes. The exercise demonstrates unsafe acceptance and metadata retention, not actual host path traversal or program execution.

name: SSRF Simulation
scenario: A support preview feature acts as a server-side intermediary to an internal synthetic document service.
objective: Enforce destination authorization at a server-side network boundary.
steps: Request GET /api/preview?source=handbook.
Change the selector to metadata.
Compare the synthetic internal classification returned by training with the hardened denial.
Confirm URL strings, IP addresses and unknown selectors are rejected without network requests.
expected: Training reaches the private synthetic fixture. Hardened allows only handbook. No variant accepts an arbitrary host, scheme, port or URL.
root_cause: The training policy lets a customer select a private internal fixture that the server can reach on their behalf.
remediation: Map approved selectors to exact server-owned URLs, allow only the public document, disable redirects and environment proxies, bound response size and time, and block Internet egress with internal networks.
residual: Unit tests use a controlled transport fixture. Only Docker execution proves actual internal service reachability and network egress boundaries. This is a constrained simulation, not arbitrary URL fetching.

name: Security Misconfiguration and Errors
owasp: A02:2025 — Security Misconfiguration; A10:2025 — Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions
scenario: A preview error exposes a synthetic source path and debug fixture, while permissive headers weaken the browser boundary.
objective: Define an error disclosure boundary and verify secure headers on error responses.
steps: Sign in and GET /api/diagnostics/error.
Inspect the body, CSP, nosniff and CORS headers.
Trigger malformed input and inspect safe validation responses.
Run the unexpected-exception test to check generic handling of actual failures.
expected: Training reveals only fixed synthetic debug values and sets wildcard CORS. Hardened returns a generic 500, a request ID and restrictive security headers without wildcard CORS.
root_cause: TrainingPolicy.error deliberately exposes debugging details and omits the hardened header policy.
remediation: Use a generic exception boundary, redact validation inputs, keep detailed event categories in structured logs, deny cross-origin sharing, and apply a consistent CSP and response header policy.
residual: The exposed path and fixture key are fabricated training data, not an actual stack trace or secret. Local HTTP provides no HSTS or TLS guarantee.
